title: The American Scholar
hook: a talk urging people to think for themselves, not only from books

segments.voice: Yesterday, the colors of the spirit: the same field looks glad or grieving depending on who crosses it. Your line was the colors of the spirit. What color did you bring today? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-one.

A hall full of educated men, gathered for a college society's yearly speech. They expect something polished about learning and books. Emerson stands up and, politely, tells them books can be a danger. Not that books are bad. That a person can read so much of other people's thinking that they forget to do any of their own. He has a name for what he wants instead, two words he keeps coming back to: Man Thinking. Not a thinker as a job title. A person, actually thinking. Today, The American Scholar.
screen: `A HALL FULL OF SCHOLARS.` → `THE DANGER IS BOOKS?` → `MAN THINKING.`

segments.voice: First, what the scholar is. In the right state, Emerson says, the scholar is Man Thinking. In the wrong state, a mere thinker, or worse, "the parrot of other men's thinking." A parrot can repeat anything. It just can't mean it. Second, what books are for. "Books are the best of things, well used; abused, among the worst." And then, even more sharply: "They are for nothing but to inspire." A book isn't meant to do your thinking. It's meant to light the fire under your own. Third, the warning, and it has humor in it. Emerson describes meek young men growing up in libraries, believing it's their duty to accept the views of the great authors, and forgetting that those great authors were once only young men in libraries too, when they wrote their books. Every famous book started as somebody thinking for themselves. Fourth, where else the scholar learns. Books are only one teacher in this talk. Emerson also names nature, the world around you, and action, actually living and working, as the scholar's schooling. Thinking for yourself doesn't mean ignoring everything that came before. It means letting what you read, what you see, and what you do all feed a mind that's actually awake. Away from lecture halls, this is small. You read a headline and you notice you've already borrowed someone's opinion of it. You hear a strong view at work and nod before you've checked whether you agree. Emerson's question isn't whether the view is right. It's whether it's yours.
screen: `MAN THINKING, NOT A PARROT.` · `BOOKS ARE FOR NOTHING BUT TO INSPIRE.` · `YOUNG MEN IN LIBRARIES.` · `NATURE, BOOKS, AND ACTION.` · then, large: `IS THE VIEW YOURS?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think one thing through yourself. Settle, and pick a question you have an opinion on, something you've mostly heard other people's answers to. Now, for these two minutes, set those voices aside. Ask: what have I actually seen? What do I actually know from my own life? Follow your own thought one step at a time, slowly. You may end up exactly where you started. That's fine. The point is that this time, you walked there. The bell holds the time.
The American Scholar. Emerson's talk calling the scholar to be Man Thinking, not the parrot of other people's thinking, with books for nothing but to inspire. Today's word.
Your line: think for myself. Today, before you repeat an opinion, ask whether you thought it or only heard it. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-one.

screen: `DAY 1191 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SNOWSTORM BEHIND THE PREACHER.`

howItsDone: Readers of The American Scholar often take its call to be 'Man Thinking' as a reminder to treat books as a spark for their own thinking rather than a substitute for it.
